quiz.why: Cytochrome c oxidase is the mitochondrial marker enzyme. Acid phosphatase marks lysosomes, glucose-6-phosphatase marks endoplasmic reticulum, and total protein tells you nothing about which organelle is present.

quiz.q: A lab reports that a new fluorescent dye lets them image a 40 nm vesicle with visible light using a conventional confocal microscope. What is the most reasonable objection?
choices: Fluorescent dyes cannot be used on vesicles
A brighter signal does not overcome the diffraction limit near 200 nm
Vesicles are too large for fluorescence imaging
quiz.why: Brightness and resolution are different things: no amount of signal makes conventional light microscopy resolve below roughly 200 nm. Dyes work fine on vesicles and confocal microscopes are fluorescence instruments, so those objections are wrong on the facts.

quiz.q: How many different amino acids are specified by the standard genetic code in human proteins?
quiz.why: Twenty amino acids are encoded. There are 64 codons in total, 61 of which specify amino acids and 3 of which are stops, and 4 is the number of nucleotide bases.

quiz.q: A reaction has a delta G of -25 kJ/mol but proceeds immeasurably slowly at body temperature. What does adding the correct enzyme accomplish?
choices: It lowers the activation energy so the same reaction reaches equilibrium much faster
It makes delta G more negative so the reaction becomes favorable
It shifts the equilibrium toward more product
It supplies energy from ATP to push the reaction forward
quiz.why: A negative delta G already means the reaction is favorable; slowness is an activation energy problem, and that is exactly what an enzyme addresses. Enzymes never change delta G, the equilibrium position, or supply energy themselves.

quiz.q: Arterial blood pH is reported as 7.20. How does this compare with the normal range and what maintains it?
choices: It is normal, maintained by the phosphate buffer system
It is alkalotic, maintained by hemoglobin alone
It is normal, maintained by lysosomal proton pumps
It is acidotic, since normal is 7.35 to 7.45, and bicarbonate is the main extracellular buffer
quiz.why: Normal arterial pH is 7.35 to 7.45, so 7.20 is acidemic, and the bicarbonate and carbon dioxide pair is the principal extracellular buffer. Phosphate buffering matters mainly inside cells, hemoglobin contributes but is not the main system, and lysosomal pumps acidify an organelle, not the blood.

quiz.q: A mutation replaces a buried valine with a charged glutamate in the core of a globular enzyme. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: No effect, because only active site residues matter
The tertiary fold is destabilized because a charged group cannot be buried away from water
The protein gains a new quaternary structure
quiz.why: The hydrophobic core exists because burying nonpolar groups is favorable; forcing a charge into it destabilizes the fold. Residues far from the active site routinely matter, the primary structure has by definition changed, and there is no reason a buried substitution would create a new subunit interface.

quiz.q: Approximately how thick is a biological lipid bilayer?
quiz.why: About 5 nm, roughly two fatty acid tails end to end. 2 nm is the width of a DNA double helix, 0.5 nm is near single-atom scale, and 50 nm would be ten times too thick.

quiz.q: Per molecule of ATP hydrolyzed, what does the Na+/K+-ATPase move?
quiz.why: Three sodium out for two potassium in makes the pump electrogenic, contributing directly to the negative interior. Equal exchange would not be electrogenic, and the reversed options would collapse the very gradients the cell needs.

quiz.q: An infant has thick airway secretions, recurrent lung infection and a sweat chloride of 88 mmol/L. What is the molecular defect?
choices: A defective chloride channel in the apical membrane
Absent dynein arms in airway cilia
quiz.why: A sweat chloride above 60 mmol/L with thick secretions is cystic fibrosis, caused by the CFTR chloride channel failing so water does not follow salt. A broken sodium pump would be lethal broadly, absent dynein arms give Kartagener syndrome without high sweat chloride, and the mannose-6-phosphate defect is I-cell disease.

quiz.q: Digoxin inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase in cardiac muscle. Why does contractility increase?
choices: Potassium accumulates inside the cell and depolarizes it
ATP is spared and directly powers more cross-bridge cycling
Calcium is pumped into the cell by the ATPase itself
Intracellular sodium rises, so the sodium-calcium exchanger slows and calcium accumulates
quiz.why: The exchanger normally uses the inward sodium gradient to expel calcium; weakening that gradient leaves more calcium inside for contraction. Intracellular potassium falls rather than accumulating, the pump moves no calcium, and sparing ATP is not the mechanism.

quiz.q: How much DNA is wrapped around a single histone octamer in a nucleosome?
quiz.why: 147 base pairs wrap about 1.65 turns around the octamer of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4. The other values do not correspond to the nucleosome core particle; 300 is closer to the width in angstroms of the 30 nm fiber, not a base pair count.

quiz.q: A somatic fibroblast line stops dividing after about 50 passages, while a tumor line divides indefinitely. What is the most likely difference?
choices: The tumor line expresses telomerase and maintains its TTAGGG repeats
The tumor line replicates its DNA conservatively
The tumor line uses only nonhomologous end joining
quiz.why: Telomerase reactivation, seen in 85-90% of cancers, rebuilds the TTAGGG repeat and removes the Hayflick limit. Replication is semiconservative in all cells, fibroblasts without ligase could not replicate at all, and the choice of double-strand break pathway does not set replicative lifespan.

quiz.q: During replication, DNA polymerase encounters the strand oriented so that the fork moves toward its 3' end. What happens on that strand?
choices: It is copied continuously as the leading strand
It is not copied until after mitosis
It is copied discontinuously in Okazaki fragments of about 100-200 nucleotides
It is copied in the 3' to 5' direction by a specialized polymerase
quiz.why: Because synthesis runs only 5' to 3', the strand oriented against the fork must be restarted repeatedly as short fragments later joined by ligase. No polymerase synthesizes 3' to 5', and both strands are copied in the same S phase.

quiz.q: A patient with xeroderma pigmentosum develops many skin cancers in childhood after minimal sun exposure. Which lesion is going unrepaired?
choices: Thymine dimers created by ultraviolet light
quiz.why: Xeroderma pigmentosum is a nucleotide excision repair defect, and UV-induced thymine dimers are its classic bulky substrate. Deaminated cytosine is handled by base excision repair, double-strand breaks by HR or NHEJ, and microsatellite slippage by mismatch repair.

quiz.q: Which modification is added to the 5' end of a eukaryotic mRNA?
choices: A poly-A tail of about 200 residues
quiz.why: The 7-methylguanosine cap protects the 5' end and is what the small ribosomal subunit recognizes. The poly-A tail goes on the 3' end, while mannose-6-phosphate and ubiquitin are protein tags, not RNA modifications.

quiz.q: A researcher deletes the N-terminal signal sequence from a secreted hormone. Where will the protein end up?
choices: In the Golgi, delivered by COPI vesicles
In the lysosome, tagged with mannose-6-phosphate
quiz.why: Without a signal sequence, SRP never binds and the ribosome finishes translation in the cytosol, so the protein never enters the secretory pathway at all. Golgi, lysosomal and plasma membrane destinations all require ER entry first.

quiz.q: Cultured cells from a child secrete lysosomal enzymes into the medium, and the cells fill with inclusions. Which enzyme activity is missing?
quiz.why: Without the mannose-6-phosphate tag, hydrolases miss the lysosome and are secreted by default, which is I-cell disease. Hexosaminidase A loss gives Tay-Sachs with one accumulated substrate, signal peptidase loss would block secretion entirely, and ubiquitin activation concerns the proteasome.

quiz.q: A mutation prevents COPI coat assembly. Which consequence follows most directly?
choices: Proteins can no longer leave the ER
Endocytosis at the plasma membrane stops
ER-resident proteins that escaped to the Golgi are not retrieved
quiz.why: COPI runs the retrograde Golgi-to-ER leg, so losing it strands escaped ER residents in the Golgi. Forward transport out of the ER is a COPII job, endocytosis is clathrin's, and misrouted lysosomal enzymes reflect a mannose-6-phosphate defect.

quiz.q: What is the diameter of a microtubule and what is its subunit?
choices: 25 nm, built from alpha and beta tubulin dimers
quiz.why: Microtubules are 25 nm hollow tubes of 13 protofilaments of alpha-beta tubulin dimers. 7 nm actin and 10 nm intermediate filaments are the other two systems, and myosin is a motor, not a filament subunit here.

quiz.q: Cargo must travel from a neuron's cell body down a long axon to the terminal. Which motor and direction?
choices: Kinesin, toward the microtubule plus end
Dynein, toward the microtubule plus end
Dynein, toward the microtubule minus end
quiz.why: Microtubule plus ends point away from the centrosome and down the axon, and kinesin walks to plus ends, giving anterograde transport. Dynein walks to minus ends for retrograde traffic, and intermediate filaments carry no motors at all.

quiz.q: A chemotherapy agent causes microtubules to become abnormally stable bundles that will not disassemble. Which agent is it?
quiz.why: Taxanes such as paclitaxel hyperstabilize microtubules, blocking the disassembly mitosis requires. Vincristine and colchicine prevent polymerization instead, and cytochalasin D caps actin filaments.

quiz.q: A man has lifelong sinus infections, bronchiectasis, dextrocardia and immotile sperm. What underlying defect explains all four findings at once?
choices: Defective axonemal dynein arms in the 9+2 axoneme
quiz.why: One machine, dynein-driven ciliary and flagellar beating, serves the airway, the embryonic node that sets left-right asymmetry, and the sperm tail, which is Kartagener syndrome. CFTR disease gives sinus and lung findings but not situs inversus, and neither keratin nor lysosomal targeting defects touch ciliary motion.

quiz.q: Which second messenger is produced when a Gs-coupled receptor is activated?
quiz.why: Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase, which makes cAMP and activates protein kinase A. IP3, DAG and the calcium release they trigger all belong to the Gq and phospholipase C branch instead.

quiz.q: Cholera toxin acts on which target, and with what effect?
choices: It blocks the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, preventing depolarization
It locks G-alpha-s in the GTP-bound state, so cAMP stays high
It cleaves SNARE proteins, preventing vesicle fusion
It inhibits phospholipase C, reducing IP3
quiz.why: Blocking Gs GTP hydrolysis leaves adenylyl cyclase permanently on, driving chloride and water into the gut lumen. SNARE cleavage describes botulinum toxin, and neither nicotinic blockade nor phospholipase C inhibition produces secretory diarrhea.

quiz.q: Epidermal growth factor binds its receptor. What is the immediate next molecular event?
choices: A trimeric G protein exchanges GDP for GTP
Two receptors dimerize and phosphorylate tyrosines on each other
The receptor opens a calcium channel in the plasma membrane
quiz.why: Receptor tyrosine kinases work by ligand-driven dimerization and trans-autophosphorylation, creating SH2 docking sites. Trimeric G proteins and adenylyl cyclase belong to GPCR signaling, and RTKs are not ion channels.

quiz.q: A patient in an asthma attack is given inhaled albuterol and improves within minutes. Which sequence explains the response?
choices: Beta-2 receptor, Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP up, airway smooth muscle relaxes
Alpha-1 receptor, Gq, IP3, calcium up, airway smooth muscle relaxes
Beta-1 receptor, Gi, cAMP down, heart rate falls
Muscarinic receptor, Gq, DAG, protein kinase C, bronchoconstriction
quiz.why: Beta-2 receptors on airway smooth muscle are Gs-coupled, so raising cAMP relaxes the muscle. Raising calcium through Gq contracts rather than relaxes smooth muscle, beta-1 effects are cardiac, and muscarinic Gq signaling is exactly what worsens bronchospasm.

quiz.q: Which statement about cyclins and CDKs is correct?
choices: CDK levels stay roughly constant while cyclin levels rise and fall
Cyclin levels stay constant while CDK levels oscillate
Both are degraded only during G0
Cyclins are kinases and CDKs are their substrates
quiz.why: The oscillation lives in the cyclin; the kinase is present but inactive until a cyclin binds. CDK is the kinase and cyclin the regulatory partner, not the reverse, and cyclin degradation happens at each transition rather than only in G0.

quiz.q: Cells irradiated in G1 arrest before S phase. Cells from a Li-Fraumeni patient with a TP53 mutation do not. Why?
choices: p53 normally phosphorylates Rb to drive arrest
p53 normally degrades cyclin B directly
p53 normally activates caspase-8 at the plasma membrane
p53 normally induces p21, a CDK inhibitor that blocks Rb phosphorylation
quiz.why: The arrest depends on p53-driven p21, which inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes and keeps Rb unphosphorylated. p53 is a transcription factor, not a kinase or a protease, and caspase-8 belongs to the extrinsic death receptor route.

quiz.q: A lymphoma overexpresses BCL-2 because of a t(14;18) translocation. What is the functional result?
choices: Cells divide faster because cyclin D is amplified
Cells resist intrinsic apoptosis because cytochrome c release is blocked
The spindle checkpoint fails and chromosomes missegregate
quiz.why: BCL-2 is anti-apoptotic and restrains BAX and BAK, so overexpression prevents mitochondrial cytochrome c release and the cells accumulate by not dying. It does not accelerate the cycle, arrest cells, or alter kinetochore attachment.

quiz.q: Human papillomavirus E7 protein binds and inactivates Rb. What is the predicted downstream effect on the cell cycle?
choices: E2F is sequestered and S phase entry is blocked
The spindle checkpoint is permanently engaged
E2F is released and S-phase genes are transcribed without growth factor signals
Cyclin B accumulates and the cell arrests in G2
quiz.why: Rb's only job in this switch is holding E2F; inactivating Rb frees E2F and lets the cell pass the restriction point without external signals. Sequestering E2F would require more Rb function, and neither the spindle checkpoint nor G2 arrest is downstream of Rb.

quiz.q: Which pairing correctly describes a tumor suppressor gene?
choices: RAS, gain of function, one allele needed
RB1, loss of function, usually both alleles needed
BCR-ABL, fusion kinase, one allele needed
quiz.why: Tumor suppressors are lost rather than activated and generally require both alleles to be hit, and RB1 is the founding example. RAS, MYC and BCR-ABL are all oncogenes that act through gain of function in a single allele.

quiz.q: A patient with chronic myeloid leukemia carries the Philadelphia chromosome. Which drug targets the resulting protein?
quiz.why: The t(9;22) translocation creates the constitutively active BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase, which imatinib inhibits. Trastuzumab targets HER2, bevacizumab targets VEGF, and paclitaxel is a nonspecific microtubule agent.

quiz.q: A lung tumor carries an activating KRAS mutation. Why is an EGFR inhibitor unlikely to help?
choices: KRAS acts downstream of EGFR, so the pathway stays on regardless of receptor blockade
KRAS mutations prevent the drug from entering the cell
EGFR inhibitors only work on tumor suppressor mutations
KRAS mutation destroys the cell's microtubules
quiz.why: Blocking a receptor cannot silence a pathway that is already switched on below it. Drug uptake is unaffected, EGFR inhibitors target an oncogenic kinase rather than a suppressor, and KRAS has nothing to do with microtubule integrity.

quiz.q: A solid tumor grows to 2 mm and then stops enlarging until a region becomes hypoxic. Which change most likely allows growth to resume?
choices: HIF-1-alpha is stabilized and induces VEGF-driven angiogenesis
quiz.why: Past roughly 1-2 mm diffusion cannot supply the tumor, and hypoxia-stabilized HIF-1-alpha turning on VEGF recruits the vessels that lift the limit. Telomerase addresses replicative lifespan not nutrient supply, rising E-cadherin would reduce invasiveness, and a stronger checkpoint would slow growth.

quiz.q: Approximately how many ATP are produced from the complete oxidation of one glucose molecule?
quiz.why: About 30 to 38 ATP, the range reflecting which shuttle carries cytosolic NADH into the mitochondrion. A net of 2 ATP is glycolysis alone, and the other values are far outside any accepted estimate.

quiz.q: A family has muscle weakness, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes. Affected mothers pass it to all children; affected fathers pass it to none. What is the mechanism?
choices: Autosomal recessive inheritance with high carrier frequency
Genomic imprinting of a nuclear gene
A mitochondrial DNA mutation, inherited only from the mother
quiz.why: Transmission exclusively through mothers is the fingerprint of mitochondrial DNA, and MELAS fits the clinical picture and the heteroplasmy-driven variability. Autosomal recessive disease passes from both parents, X-linked dominant disease passes from fathers to all daughters, and imprinted nuclear genes still come from both parents.

quiz.q: You want to know whether a treatment changed the total amount and apparent size of a protein in a cell lysate. Which technique answers that?
choices: Flow cytometry with a DNA stain
quiz.why: A western blot separates proteins by size and detects one with an antibody, reporting both abundance and apparent molecular weight. qPCR measures transcript rather than protein, a DNA-stain flow profile reports cell cycle distribution, and SEM shows surface topography.

quiz.q: Cardiac muscle cells contract as a coordinated unit because an electrical signal passes directly from one cell to the next. Which junction is responsible?
quiz.why: Gap junctions are connexon pores that let ions and molecules under about 1,000 daltons pass directly between cells, electrically coupling them. Tight junctions seal the space between cells, and desmosomes and hemidesmosomes provide mechanical anchoring only.

scenarios.title: Problem set: a secreted protein that will not leave the cell
scenarios.intro:
Your instructor puts a case on the board. A lab studies a secreted hormone. In wild-type cells the protein appears in the culture medium within 30 minutes. In a mutant line the medium is empty, but total protein measured in whole-cell lysate is unchanged, and the mutant protein runs about 2 kilodaltons larger on a gel than the wild-type secreted form.

You are asked to design experiments that localize the block and name the step that failed. Reason from the secretory pathway, one step at a time.

steps.prompt: Start with what the data already tell you. Total protein is normal, but nothing is secreted and the mutant runs larger. What is the best first inference?

choices.text: Synthesis is intact, so the defect lies in targeting or transport, and the extra 2 kilodaltons suggests an uncleaved signal sequence
choices.feedback: Correct. Normal total protein rules out a transcription or translation failure, and a signal sequence of roughly 16-30 residues is about the right mass to explain a 2 kilodalton difference.

choices.text: The gene is not being transcribed, so start with qPCR for the message
choices.feedback: Unchanged total protein already rules this out. qPCR is not wrong to run as a control, but it cannot be the primary hypothesis when the protein is demonstrably present.

choices.text: The protein is being made but degraded immediately by the proteasome
choices.feedback: Plausible-sounding but inconsistent with the data. Rapid degradation would lower total protein, and it would not make the remaining band run larger.

steps.prompt: You want to know where in the cell the mutant protein is sitting. Which experiment gives you location most directly?

choices.text: Western blot the whole-cell lysate at several time points
choices.feedback: This tells you amount and size over time, which is useful, but a whole-cell lysate has no spatial information at all. It cannot distinguish cytosol from ER lumen.

choices.text: Express a fluorescent fusion of the protein and image it by confocal microscopy alongside an ER marker
choices.feedback: Right. Only imaging answers where. Co-staining with an ER marker turns a vague signal into an answer, and confocal sectioning keeps out-of-focus haze from faking colocalization.

choices.text: Run flow cytometry on the cells with a DNA stain
choices.feedback: That reports cell cycle distribution one cell at a time. It has nothing to say about subcellular localization of a protein.

steps.prompt: The fusion protein is diffusely cytosolic, with no ER colocalization at all. What does that finding rule in?

choices.text: A COPII coat defect trapping cargo inside the ER
choices.feedback: A COPII failure traps cargo in the ER lumen, so you would see bright ER signal. Diffuse cytosol means the protein never got into the ER in the first place.

choices.text: The protein never entered the ER, so the failure is at signal sequence recognition or translocation
choices.feedback: Correct, and it fits the size shift. If SRP cannot bind the signal sequence, translation finishes in the cytosol and signal peptidase never clips the sequence off.

choices.text: Mannose-6-phosphate tagging failed, so the protein went to the cytosol
choices.feedback: Losing that tag misroutes lysosomal enzymes to secretion, not to the cytosol, and it acts in the cis-Golgi, long after ER entry. The location does not fit.

steps.prompt: To prove the signal sequence is the problem, you propose a swap experiment. Which construct makes the cleanest test?

choices.text: Delete the mutant's first 30 residues entirely and see whether secretion returns
choices.feedback: Deletion removes the sequence rather than repairing it, so the predicted result is still no secretion. A negative result would not distinguish your hypothesis from several others.

choices.text: Replace the mutant signal sequence with a known functional signal sequence from a different secreted protein
choices.feedback: Correct. If a borrowed working signal sequence restores secretion, the rest of the protein and the rest of the pathway are fine, and the defect is localized to that sequence.

choices.text: Add a nuclear localization signal to the mutant protein
choices.feedback: That tests importin-mediated nuclear entry, a different pathway. It would move the protein into the nucleus and tell you nothing about ER targeting.

steps.prompt: The swap restores secretion. A classmate asks how you would have interpreted a different result: the mutant protein showing bright ER signal and never reaching the Golgi. Which explanation would you have favored, and how would you test it?

choices.text: A COPII coat or cargo-receptor defect blocking the forward ER-to-Golgi step, tested by imaging a Golgi marker and checking sugar processing
choices.feedback: Right. Cargo stuck in the ER points to the forward vesicle step, and Golgi-specific sugar modifications would be absent, giving a second independent line of evidence.

choices.text: A COPI defect, since COPI vesicles carry cargo from the ER to the Golgi
choices.feedback: The directions are reversed. COPII carries cargo forward from ER to Golgi; COPI runs the retrograde leg back.

choices.text: Misfolding causing ER retention and ER-associated degradation, tested by asking whether a proteasome inhibitor restores protein levels
choices.feedback: A reasonable alternative worth ruling out, since misfolded protein is held in the ER and retro-translocated for destruction. It is a real competing hypothesis, just not the first one this picture suggests.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern to carry away is that localization questions are answered by imaging, abundance and size questions by blotting, and causation only by a swap or rescue experiment. Reading the secretory pathway in order gives you a checklist: does the protein get into the ER at all, does it leave the ER, does it get its Golgi modifications, does it get the right address tag. A 2 kilodalton size shift in a secreted protein should immediately make you think of an uncleaved signal sequence, because that sequence is roughly 16 to 30 residues long and signal peptidase normally removes it on entry.

scenarios.title: Problem set: reading a checkpoint experiment in a tumor line
scenarios.intro:
A second case goes on the board. Two cell lines are irradiated with the same dose. Line A is a normal fibroblast line. Line B comes from a tumor in a patient with a family history of early sarcoma and breast cancer. Six hours after irradiation you have a western blot for p53 and p21, and flow cytometry DNA-content profiles for both lines.

Line A shows p53 protein rising sharply, p21 rising with it, and a flow profile with cells piling up at 2n DNA content. Line B shows no rise in p53 or p21 and a flow profile essentially unchanged from baseline. Work out what each result means before you name the gene.

steps.prompt: First: in line A, p53 protein rises within hours but the lab confirms TP53 transcription did not change. How is that possible?

choices.text: p53 is normally degraded rapidly by MDM2-driven ubiquitination, and damage-activated ATM and ATR stabilize it
choices.feedback: Correct. p53 is regulated mostly by protein stability, not by transcription, which is exactly how a cell gets a fast response to damage without waiting on gene expression.

choices.text: The antibody must be cross-reacting; protein cannot rise without transcription rising
choices.feedback: Protein level is set by synthesis minus degradation, so slowing degradation raises the level with no change in transcription. This is a common reasoning slip worth naming out loud.

choices.text: Translation of existing p53 mRNA increased
choices.feedback: Translational control is a real mechanism and not absurd here, but the established and dominant route for p53 is stabilization of protein that was being destroyed.

steps.prompt: Line A's flow profile piles cells at 2n DNA content. What does that mean, and which p53 target explains it?

choices.text: Cells arrested in G2 with 4n DNA, explained by cyclin B degradation
choices.feedback: The DNA content does not match. A G2 arrest piles cells at 4n, not 2n, because the genome has already been copied.

choices.text: Cells arrested in G1 with an unreplicated 2n genome, explained by p21 inhibiting cyclin-CDK and keeping Rb unphosphorylated
choices.feedback: Right. 2n means DNA has not been copied yet, so the block is before S phase, and p21 is the CDK inhibitor that enforces it by preventing Rb phosphorylation.

choices.text: Cells are undergoing apoptosis, shown by the 2n peak
choices.feedback: Apoptotic cells with fragmented DNA appear as a sub-2n peak below the G1 population, not at 2n. Watch which side of the G1 peak the signal sits on.

steps.prompt: Line B shows neither p53 nor p21 induction and no arrest. Before blaming p53 itself, what is the alternative you must exclude?

choices.text: Nothing: absent p21 proves TP53 is mutated
choices.feedback: Too fast. p21 sits downstream of p53, so its absence is equally consistent with a p53 problem and with an upstream sensing problem.

choices.text: That the upstream damage sensors ATM and ATR are defective, so p53 is never stabilized even though the gene is intact
choices.feedback: Correct. A downstream failure and an upstream sensing failure look identical on this blot, which is why the experiment cannot stop here.

choices.text: That the radiation dose was too low to cause damage in line B
choices.feedback: Worth controlling and cheap to check with a damage marker, but both lines received the same dose, so this is a control rather than the main competing hypothesis.

steps.prompt: Which single experiment best separates a broken p53 from a broken upstream sensor?

choices.text: Introduce wild-type p53 into line B and repeat the irradiation, asking whether p21 induction and G1 arrest return
choices.feedback: Correct. A rescue experiment is the cleanest logic available: if supplying the suspect protein restores the phenotype, the defect was in that protein.

choices.text: Sequence TP53 in line B
choices.feedback: Useful and often done first in practice, but sequence alone shows a variant, not whether that variant causes the failure. Pair it with a functional test.

choices.text: Treat line B with paclitaxel and look for mitotic arrest
choices.feedback: That probes the spindle checkpoint, a different checkpoint entirely, and tells you nothing about the G1 DNA damage response.

steps.prompt: Restoring wild-type p53 restores p21 induction and G1 arrest in line B. Given the family history of early sarcoma and breast cancer, what is the final interpretation?

choices.text: A germline TP53 mutation, that is Li-Fraumeni syndrome, with the tumor having lost the remaining wild-type allele
choices.feedback: Correct on both levels. The family pattern points to an inherited first hit in every cell, and the tumor's complete loss of function is the classic second hit at a tumor suppressor.

choices.text: An activating RAS mutation driving proliferation past the checkpoint
choices.feedback: RAS is an oncogene driving growth signaling, and it does not abolish p53 stabilization or p21 induction. The rescue experiment already pointed at p53.

choices.text: Loss of Rb, releasing E2F and overriding the arrest
choices.feedback: Rb loss would indeed push cells into S phase, but it would not silence p53 and p21 induction on the blot, and adding back p53 would not have rescued arrest.

scenarios.debrief: Two habits are the point of this case. First, read a flow cytometry profile by DNA content before naming a phase: 2n is G1, 4n is G2 or M, a sub-2n peak is apoptotic debris. Second, a blot showing an absent downstream product never by itself localizes the lesion, because everything upstream of that product is an equally good suspect, and only a rescue experiment settles it. The biology to carry away is the chain itself: damage activates ATM and ATR, which stabilize p53 by blocking its MDM2-driven destruction, and p53 induces p21, which inhibits cyclin-CDK, keeps Rb unphosphorylated, holds E2F, and stops the cell in G1. An inherited defect anywhere in that chain, most famously germline TP53 in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, produces early cancers across many tissues.
